 Screen K-town movie picks to enjoy with the little ones this Children’s Day
 By Ankita Chandra 
 Published: 14 Nov 2026, 3:14PM | 3 min read My Daughter is a Zombie
 Advertisement Korean entertainment, with its vibrant stories full of warmth and innocence, as well as its luminous and colourful musical world appeals not just to teens and young adults, but to children as well, making them hum along to the K-pop title tracks and collect posters of their favourite idols and actors right from their foundational years. This Children’s Day, t2ONLINE picks five K-town movies full of laughter and sweet moments for little ones to enjoy. 
 Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs 
 A funny and entertaining parody of the classic Snow White plot,  Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs  features seven princes who are cursed to look like dwarfs whenever people look at them. To return to their original form, they must find the most beautiful girl in the world. Meanwhile, the Snow White-inspired protagonist stumbles upon a pair of mysterious red heels, and finds herself transformed into a slender and beautiful woman on wearing them. When she crosses paths with the dwarf princes, they team up to find Snow White’s father, while every one of the princes keeps hoping that Snow White’s “true love’s kiss” would break his curse. A story about learning to love oneself irrespective of flaws, and to perceive someone for who they are from within and not from without, this animated parody of the familiar fairytale is a fun as well as illuminating watch for children.  
 The Larva Island Movie 
 Advertisement 
 A continuation of the two-part  Larva Island  series,  The Larva Island Movie  tells the story of Chuck, a man who returns to civilisation after being shipwrecked on an island for five years. In an interview with a reporter, he reveals how his return was facilitated by a chaotic insect duo named Red and Yellow. From a tribal larva named Mango to a singing seal named Clara, and a mechanical, shape-shifting creature called “Crabsformer”, Chuck recounts all the non-human friends he had met on the island when he was trying to survive the shipwreck. Full of slapstick comedy and entertaining interactions between these unique characters,  The Larva Island Movie  will surely keep the little ones laughing till the very last scene. 
 The Way Home 
 A story that highlights the tender bond between children and their grandparents,  The Way Home  follows Sang-woo, a boy who is reluctant to leave his urban life in Seoul to live with his mute grandmother in the countryside. Compelled by his mother, however, he has to go there, as she is searching for a new job. Initially, the child is highly disrespectful of his grandmother, insulting her with mean epithets and even stealing from her to buy batteries for his toy. Over time, however, understanding her unconditional love towards him, Sang-woo begins to admire and respect his grandmother, and the two form a deep bond. A story that brings children closer to their elderly loved ones,  The Way Home  is a deep and nostalgic watch. 
 Advertisement My Daughter is a Zombie 
 A story that can be enjoyed on the occasions of Children’s Day as well as Fathers’ Day,  My Daughter is a Zombie  is a comic, thrilling as well as emotional tale of a father’s struggle against society and humanity to protect his daughter. When a zombie virus breaks out and bites Su-a, the daughter of the pro animal trainer Jeong-hwan, he takes her into hiding at his childhood residence to protect her from the government’s zombie elimination drives. Attempting to train her back into humanity by using his animal-taming skills, the father plans to domesticate the daughter. In a highly emotional climax, Su-a restores her humanity as she sheds tears at the sight of her father’s sacrifice to protect her from the administrators, leading to a poignant ending which will surely make children hug their dads a little tighter every time they go out of their way to protect their little ones! 
 Minari 
 A semi-autobiographical American drama about a Korean family moving to Arkansas to start a farm of their own, Minari paints a nostalgic picture of 1980s rural America. Jacob Yi and his wife Monica dream of starting a farm of their own as they move to rural Arkansas with their young son, who has a heart condition, and young daughter. When they face financial difficulties in sustaining their ambition, they bring in Soon-ja, Monica’s mother, who is at first resented by the children for her eccentric habits like watching wrestling and swearing, which are contrary to how a “normal” American grandmother should behave. Through several challenges and the threat of separation, the family finally upholds its strength as they stay united and resilient in spite of life’s vicissitudes.
